newsitem.title: JAPAN: Impact of yen's surge on Japan stocks seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Impact of yen's surge on Japan stocks seen limited.

text.p: The yen's sharp advance to a four-month high against the dollar hit shares of leading Japanese exporters on Monday, but analysts said the impact on the stock market would likely be limited.

The slide by exporters' shares briefly dragged down the key Nikkei 225 share average to a morning low of 19,560.06, but it later bounced back sharply to end the day up 340.73 points, or 1.72 percent, at 20,143.51.
"Blue-chip shares lost ground (on the currency rally), but it is providing a chance for fresh buying on dips," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.

Shares of major blue-chip exporters fell sharply after the dollar was knocked down to around 117.60 yen in early Asian trade -- its lowest level in nearly four months -- from its New York close of around 120.25 yen on Friday.
The dollar later recovered to around 119 yen in Tokyo afternoon trading.
Japanese exporters have benefitted from the yen's weakness in the past two years, as a weak yen generally makes exported products more price competitive.
Japanese car giant Toyota Motor Corp fell 80 yen to 3,740 on the yen's renewed strength, while Honda Motor Co Ltd's share price also shed 80 yen to stand at 3,950.
Leading consumer electronics firm Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd slid 50 yen to 2,170, and top printer maker Canon Inc dropped 100 yen to 3,000, both in heavy volume trading.

The Nikkei's recovery came after buying in import-reliant sectors such as pulp/paper and oil, which benefit from a stronger yen as it cuts the cost of raw materials, overwhelmed selling of shares in exporters, brokers said.
Ishijima said the Nikkei's downside would be limited to around 19,500, while others said the average may move into a consolidation phase after a recent solid recovery.
Analysts said the yen's current strength alone would not dull the lustre of export-oriented blue chips, and added that many traders remained eager to snatch then up at cheaper levels.
"Brokers' own long positions have swollen sharply recently, but they have already unloaded them. So it is likely they will resume buying soon," Okasan's Ishijima said.

Some brokers said they did not expect the dollar to fall much below 115 yen. They said its slide was largely due to talking down of the dollar by Japanese financial authorities, which had raised speculation that the Bank of Japan might sell dollars to halt its two-year advance against the yen.

"The current forex movements were manipulated by the financial authorities, and we see the dollar's bottom at around 115 yen," said Hitoshi Morimura, chief portfolio manager at Meiji Life Insurance Co's equity department.

Ishijima said that as long as the dollar stayed around current levels, exporters' profits would not be severely hurt as many firms were using a dollar rate of 115 to 120 yen in making earnings estimates for the first half of this fiscal year.
Brokers said market sentiment had improved greatly since the Nikkei average broke back through the 20,000 barrier on Tuesday.
"The 19,500 line is seen as a tentative floor for the Nikkei average," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said.
